The corridor behind them looked longer than before, the corner they had just turned already swallowed up in the dark. Dwight pushed water-soaked hair back from his face and steadied himself, pushing on to follow David down the hallway. And behind them, the water followed. Slow. Steady. Inevitable. The second-floor hallway was dry. Mostly. A few dark puddles gleamed near the warped window frames, but it hadn’t reached here yet. Not enough to matter. Danny lounged on the upper landing with all the practiced sprawl of a bored cat; one knee hooked over the balustrade and the other braced against the cracked drywall like a king surveying his flooded kingdom. His phone was in his hand, angled down, its screen throwing a faint glow up against his mask. His robes pooled around him, dry and settled, the long straps gently fluttering around him, as if She was enjoying the show by his side. Below him, the school was doing something genuinely impressive. He'd seen Her work before. Watched domains shift, watched geometry go quietly wrong in ways that took survivors too long to notice. But this was more deliberate than usual — the hallways stretching, the furniture piling itself well beyond the random junk he'd tossed down the stairs earlier, the water rising with that particular patient quality of something that had already decided how this ended and was just filling in the middle parts. She was definitely enjoying Herself tonight. That much was obvious. On the feed, a grainy-green lens tracked the survivors below. The RC submarine had been an impulse purchase — spotted in a novelty shop in someone's memory of a boardwalk, bought on the vague suspicion that it might be funny someday. He hadn't anticipated how funny. The camera he'd rigged to it wasn't anything special, cheap night vision that turned everything a washed-out green, but it was picking up every inch of Dwight Fairfield flinching away from something he couldn't see as he circled the man’s ankles like a curious shark, and that was frankly more than enough. The camera feed swayed with the current, too slow to track at first, until it bumped into something. He flicked the rudder, turned the camera angle, and watched as Dwight jumped again — probably thought he felt a tail. Danny snorted softly into the darkness. “Fucking priceless.” He zoomed in, casually, as Dwight flailed sideways into the wall, barely muffling his own shout. Every kick, every flail, every panicked gasp was caught on film. Poor quality, sure, but the emotions read clear. Fear didn’t need 4K. “Welcome back to Night Watch,” he murmured to no one, the corners of his mouth twitching in amusement. “I’m your host, Danny 'Fuck Around and Find Out' Johnson. Let’s check in on our contestants.” He stretched a little, back cracking. Took a lazy look down the hall through his phones own camera. The school was twisting all on its own now. He didn't need to chase them. Didn't need to do anything, really — She had renovated the entire school into something these two were never getting out of on their own, and all he had to do was sit here and document the experience. He even had night vision mode on his phone for if they eventually made it upstairs. He had footage already that was genuinely some of his best work. And somewhere below him, in the dark and the rising water, Dwight Fairfield was standing very still and trying very hard not to make any noise about whatever had just grazed his knee. He adjusted the camera angle one more time, getting a better view of the pipe hallway, and settled back against the wall with a comfortable sigh. Easiest trial he'd had in years. No knives today. No hooks. Just patience, petty vengeance, and a camera. And eventually, he would wander back to his safe spot for the night with a fantastic new film for his collection, while the Entity rested from the finest meal she’s had in ages. He adjusted the angle with a lazy finger flick and watched the chaos bloom below like algae, murky, aimless, choking. Chapter Three: Surface Tension The water had risen to their shoulders, making forward progress a tense, miserable slog. Dwight kicked gently to keep his head above the surface, the motion strange and clumsy. kept one hand on the pipes running along the wall, using them to pull himself forward against the current rather than fight it directly. It was slow, but it was the only thing keeping him upright. He was tall enough to stay grounded if he really stretched, but David wasn’t so lucky — the man was full-on treading water, eyes narrowed in concentration as he tried to keep from bumping into any more unseen furniture drifting beneath them. The current tugged at Dwight's legs, lazy and persistent, and his jacket clung to him like a wet towel, dragging him down. Every stroke felt heavier. Slower. The pockets were sodden, and the soaked fabric pulled at his arms as he reached for the pipes lining the walls, trying to orient himself. “This is stupid,” he muttered, breath ragged. “This is so stupid.” He reached for another pipe — nearly missed — and yanked himself sideways just in time to avoid colliding with a floating end-table. He grabbed the next pipe junction, steadied himself, and noticed that he was slower than he'd been ten minutes ago. Slower and lower. Somewhere behind him, David grunted. The sound was swallowed a little by the dark, but still audible. The flashlight’s beam — barely hanging on — flickered again as it caught on the edge of a floating chair, then skipped off into empty space. Something bumped against Dwight’s thigh. He didn’t scream.
